content.title: About
content.content: Mozzarella is a semi‑soft Italian cheese made from cow’s or buffalo’s milk. It is known for its mild, slightly elastic texture and delicate milky flavor. The cheese is commonly used in salads, pizza, pasta dishes, and as a standalone snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditional mozzarella production involves stretching the curd in hot water, giving the cheese its characteristic fibrous structure.
The word “mozzarella” comes from the Italian “mozzare,” meaning “to cut off,” referring to the process of separating the whey.
Buffalo mozzarella is considered richer and creamier than the cow‑milk version.
Mozzarella is a key ingredient in the Caprese salad, paired with tomatoes, basil, and olive oil.
The cheese has a high moisture content (about 50 %), so it should be kept refrigerated in an airtight package to prevent drying out.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Mozzarella provides a good amount of calcium, essential for bone and dental health.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: The cheese supplies high‑quality dairy protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: It contains vitamins B2 (riboflavin) and B12, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Lower sodium compared to many cheeses
items.content: Mozzarella typically has less salt than many other cheeses, making it a moderate‑sodium option.

items.title: Probiotic properties
items.content: Live cultures in mozzarella can contribute to a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People with lactose intolerance may experience digestive discomfort after eating mozzarella.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Allergic reactions to casein or whey can occur in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Mozzarella contains saturated fats; those monitoring cholesterol should watch portion sizes.

items.title: Shelf life
items.content: The cheese loses freshness quickly; discard it if it develops a sour smell or mold.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Mozzarella can be enjoyed fresh, sliced into salads, melted on pizza and casseroles, or served with olive oil and herbs. For a softer texture, let it come to room temperature before serving.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store mozzarella in the refrigerator in an airtight container, submerged in lightly salted water or its own brine. When kept properly, it stays fresh for 5‑7 days.
